The Morriss Estate. The lane ran deep; from the ground floors of the houses on either side came wave upon wave of the smell of frying oil. In some household or other a child suddenly burst out squalling, and then, a moment later, everything sank back into silence.

Yi Junnian looked up at one of the houses. The curtains were drawn, a lamp was lit within, and it threw into relief the shadow of the flowers on the sill. A vase of flowers was the safe signal. He went round to the end of the lane and pushed open a door that stood ajar. It was the back door; inside was the kitchen, empty just now, for the several ground-floor tenants had finished cooking and gone into their rooms.
He went straight up to the second floor and knocked, and Ling Wen opened the door.

Yi Junnian took off his overcoat and hung it on the teakwood hat-and-coat stand by the door. On the table stood the meal she had just made: pork slices stir-fried with bean sprouts, a pig's-trotter and soybean soup, and stewed radish.

“Have the people downstairs asked you where you've been lately?” Yi Junnian asked her. Ling Wen was the second landlord. Some years before, Long Dong had taken the lease on this lane house and, choosing an auspicious day, moved her in. The two of them were husband and wife, and so settled into their surroundings more easily than those comrades who lived together as a sham married couple only because the work required it. Unlike comrades working in the other systems, Long Dong had gone underground to do intelligence work for the Party before the Kuomintang showed its true face. On the eve of the April Twelfth massacre, many comrades, caught up in the high tide of the National Revolution, had taken the enemy too lightly; and though Long Dong's cell was well hidden, it had not been kept wholly apart from the Party's open activities, and so it too was broken up when the Kuomintang launched its wholesale purge of the Communists. The enemy, however, never discovered this house.

“I said I'd gone to stay a few days with relatives,” Ling Wen told Yi Junnian over the meal. “I think they may know. Little Bao downstairs says strangers came to the house asking questions, with Detective Yao of the Municipal Police along with them. Wasn't it this same Detective Yao who led the constables charging into the market that day?”

Anyone who had read the novel Ling Wen wrote, Winter, would have supposed that she and Long Dong could scarcely be told apart. No one would ever have guessed that he could go, just like that, without their so much as seeing each other one last time. The liaison station had been blown; the agents burst soundlessly into the room while Ling Wen was there collecting a letter, and she was seized along with the rest. Mercifully the secret letter had been destroyed. Ling Wen was not on the arrest list; the agents did not know she too was a member of the cell, and after a few months they let her go. But by the time she came out of prison, Long Dong had vanished, and nearly everything connected with him had disappeared along with him.
“I'm afraid that one day you'll suddenly be gone, like water running into the sea.”
“Then face the sea, and you'll see me.”
This was an exchange between the pair of lovers in the novel (she had given them her own name and Long Dong's). One morning the Wen of the novel told the Dong that she had had a terrible dream.

A year and more later came word that Long Dong had been killed. Ling Wen could not find the organization; but the house had been leased in the couple's own names and had never been exposed, and under Shanghai's rules of tenancy an owner could not cancel a lease and take back a house without cause. The rent rose month by month, and she found that so long as she sublet a portion of the rooms she could go on living there. When Yi Junnian found her and brought her back to work, she did in fact raise the idea of giving up the lease, but Yi Junnian would not have it. This house, he said, has never once been used as a liaison station; even our own comrades scarcely know of it. Since it costs the organization nothing, why not go on living here? It may serve a purpose one day. In truth she did not want to leave either, because of Long Dong.
“What did the Municipal Police have to say?” Yi Junnian asked.
“If there were anything important, they'd tell me. I'm on good terms with the neighbors here.”
“That's because you don't raise the rent.”
“Of course I can't raise it. We mustn't play the exploiting class.”
“A second landlord who's unlike every other second landlord, that's just the sort of thing that makes people suspicious.”
“All the same, I won't put the rent up.”

Yi Junnian nodded and swore in jest with a laugh: “That little hooligan Bao, polite enough to his neighbors, at least.” He meant the ground-floor tenant Wu Sibao, who had once been a groom at the racecourse until a foreign gentleman on the racecourse board took a liking to him and picked him out to be a chauffeur. Bao had seized the chance and made himself a going concern all round the racecourse; out on the streets they all called him “Morriss Little Bao.”
“They're all like that. A rabbit doesn't eat the grass by its own burrow, they say.”
“I saw the man sent down from above this afternoon,” he said, ladling soup into his rice bowl.
“Isn't that a little risky?” They had only just been released; by the ordinary principles of underground work, the Party ought to observe a silent period before making contact with such people again.

“Perhaps it's because the assignment is very urgent; that's why they called the meeting together at short notice in the first place. The thing is, the comrade sent down from above to pass on the assignment never appeared either.” Yi Junnian stirred the soup twice with his spoon, then set the bowl down. “Old Fang has been killed too.”

Ling Wen was deeply grieved. And beyond the grief, she vaguely blamed herself. In the lockup she had made up her mind at the last and written that secret letter. To bring the secret letterbox back into use after her arrest had been most improper. The moment the letter passed into Miss Tao's hands she had begun to regret it. She had gone on wondering whether she had committed some grave error; she felt Old Fang's death was bound up with that letter.

“In secret work you must think everything through beforehand, but there's no use dwelling on it now,” Yi Junnian said absently, his mind seemingly on some other matter. He was often like this, and Ling Wen, who had seen it many times, thought nothing of it. They were both people who could work a thing out clearly in their heads; she could not. When she wanted to think a matter through in earnest, she always wanted to take up a pen and write it down. People differ: at the very same work of the mind Old Yi could look as if his thoughts were miles away, and so she sometimes felt that when Yi Junnian did not want to answer a question, he would put on that absent air.

It was thanks to Yi Junnian that she had been able to re-establish contact with the Party. Like Long Dong, Yi Junnian too commanded a secret intelligence network. Old Fang used to say that Old Yi had planted his aerial in the very heart of the enemy, that with one Yi Junnian their security work was half taken care of. The municipal Party headquarters, the police department, the Municipal Police, Old Yi could get intelligence out of them all. Often in the dead of night Old Yi would hurry to her place, hand her a cigarette or a wax pellet, tell her that someone was in danger, and require her to send the intelligence out that same night. At such times she always felt proud of the work she and the comrades of the cell were doing.
“What's this?”
Yi Junnian had finished eating and sat on the sofa smoking. He picked up a small scrap of paper from beside the tea tray and stared at it a while. Ling Wen, a cloth in her hand, came over to look.
“Just idle scribbling.”

She had a habit of scribbling on whatever paper came to hand: fully formed ideas went into a little notebook, odds and ends of thought onto scraps. A sheet of manuscript paper cut into a small pad, kept in her pocket. On this scrap were written the words “mole” and “dice,” and a jumble of doodles that no one could have made out.
“You must break yourself of this habit,” Yi Junnian said. “It's very dangerous.”
He struck a match and burned the scrap in the ashtray.
“I'm sure there's a mole. Couldn't we find some lead from inside the enemy?”

Yi Junnian drew a deep pull on his cigarette and said slowly: “I'll look into it. If my suspicion is right, this mole must be very deeply hidden; even on the enemy's side only a handful of people would know of him.”
“Have you anyone in mind?”
“Don't be too quick to suspect a comrade.” Yi Junnian looked at her and said sternly, “Branding comrades moles at the drop of a hat, we've paid a bitter price for that before.”
“If we don't root him out, the organization will suffer even greater damage.”
The remark went straight to what was troubling Yi Junnian. From the way today's contact had gone, the higher-ups must be harboring suspicions too.

“Why do you think the enemy released us this time?” he asked Ling Wen idly, aimlessly, even as he turned it over in his mind. He had not managed to find Old Fang, but he had sought out Wei Dafu. After fleeing that day, Wei Dafu had slipped into the market crowd, happened upon an acquaintance, and hurried up to strike up a conversation, using it as cover to get out of the market building. After he got away, Wei Dafu seemed to have gone looking for Old Fang.
“You don't believe what Wei Dafu says?”

“Perhaps, perhaps—” Yi Junnian mused. “Think of it: so much happened in the market that day. Someone fired a gun, someone jumped from a window, someone ran. It was supposed to be gambling, yet there was no money on the table. Would the agents believe our story? The organization can find connections, get people to intercede for a rescue; but if the agents truly believed the people in their hands were Communists, would they let us go?”
“Release us for show, and keep us under watch and follow us?”
“Weren't you the one suspecting we've been penetrated from within?” Yi Junnian gazed at her.
“If you don't believe what Wei Dafu says—” the thought struck Ling Wen suddenly, “do you think he sold out Old Fang?”

A wind had risen, and the room was a little cold at night. Yi Junnian sat on the sitting-room sofa; Ling Wen fetched the thermos from the next room and made him a cup of tea. As he took the cup, Ling Wen saw the scar of a burn on his wrist and reached out to touch it lightly. There was a question in her mind she had never found the chance to ask him—
“You mentioned to me once that Old Fang said the man sent down from above would produce a pair of dice.”
Yi Junnian fixed his eyes on the photograph on the tea table, the small picture frame that had once stood on the dressing table.

“The agents seem to have known about it,” Ling Wen said slowly, as though setting her thoughts in order. “When that Captain You interrogated Young Dong, he asked specially about the dice, and when he came bursting in he produced a pair of dice himself. Didn't they question you about it?”
“What is it you want to know?” Yi Junnian looked at her gravely.

“When the agents came in, I saw you with the dice in your hand; you put them in your own pocket. For a moment I was quite confused. So the comrade sent down from above to pass on the assignment was you. Later, once I was in the lockup, I never stopped worrying about you.”
“That's the biggest problem of all. That they knew about the dice means they understand the Party's secret arrangements, and yet in the end they let us go.”

Yi Junnian sank into thought. Ling Wen knew she must not disturb him now: Old Yi had a wealth of intelligence experience and a gift for spotting the faintest trace, catching a thread-end from a stray word or two, and reasoning his way, step by step, to the truth.

At times like this, watching him, she would feel in a daze that he was a little like Long Dong. Though when she thought it over carefully, she felt the two were not the same kind of man at all. Long Dong was expansive; the more urgent the situation, the looser and easier he grew. Yi Junnian, she remembered once telling him so herself, the moment he met with an emergency he would grow fretful and on edge, and if someone spoke, cut in with a word, he might even lose his temper. It was that very time that she had first mentioned Long Dong in front of him, and it had nearly ended badly; had there not been business to see to just then, he might have swept out in a huff.

At dusk she had taken the photograph and sat on the sofa a long while, remembering. That summer Long Dong had brought home a small Leica camera, and the two of them had gone off together to Hongkou Park; he loaded the film and took several photographs of her. There are pictures like these at the head of the roll, Long Dong said, they make good cover. He even went and talked a Jew in a soft felt cap into taking one of the two of them together. The Jew had been standing on the grass, playing and singing, holding a curious three-stringed instrument whose body was not round but made in the shape of a triangle. The Jew took their picture and then played and sang the whole thing over again, just for the two of them. Afterward Long Dong told her the instrument was called a ba-la-lai-ka, teaching her to say the word one syllable at a time, and that the tune was called tum-ba-la-lai-ka, which meant the playing of that very instrument. It was a Yiddish folk song, and out on the empty park lawn it sounded especially melancholy and moving; to this day she could still hum that refrain, tum-bala, tum-balalaika.

These were things Old Yi would never do. That was how she was, forever setting the two men side by side. Sometimes the more she compared them the more alike they seemed; sometimes the more she compared them the less alike. At their work the two were simply too alike. Ling Wen often felt that if the two of them had worked on the same line, they would surely have understood each other perfectly. They both thought about problems in a way unlike other people's, skipping over certain things to seize the conclusion directly. Walking along, they would suddenly seem to remember something and whip their heads around, so that anyone tailing them from behind would be caught out. When they met her somewhere, they would leave abruptly on parting, as if a sentence were left unfinished and the person had vanished like a dream. Even the way the two of them spoke was alike: from setting out a secret task to idle daily chatter, there was no need for any transition or turn at all, and even a sudden drop of the voice seemed perfectly natural. Several times, in fact, Ling Wen found that in arranging a way to make contact, or inventing a cover story, Yi Junnian would hit on the very same idea Long Dong had, years before.

“At the interrogation they questioned me, so they used the electric torture. Once they did, I was actually reassured; it meant they had no other means, that they were at the end of their rope. Someone had put the dice on the table, and that means the comrade sent down from above is among us.”

Once more Yi Junnian saw the photograph on the tea table, and he wondered: if Long Dong had met with such a situation, would he too have decided on the spot like this? “The moment things turned chaotic outside, I decided at once to take the dice. No one knows who this comrade is; I don't know either, and that's for the best. With the dice on me, if the enemy should get wind of the arrangement, I can say I am the one who carried them.

“I trust myself to hold out under the enemy's interrogation. Besides, I really don't know what the assignment actually is. This way, the Party's most important secret is kept safe. In the lockup I did not tell them the truth, because I did not know whether ‘Old Kai’ was among us prisoners, nor whether there was a planted agent in our midst. I ran through every possibility: both men in prison, both escaped, or one inside and one out. Whatever the case, my only choice was to pretend that I myself was the comrade sent down from above.”
“‘Old Kai’?”
“The comrade sent down from above,” Yi Junnian hesitated, “—his code name is ‘Old Kai.’”
“But when the enemy questioned me, they only ever asked about Haohan,” Ling Wen blurted out.

“So it seems the enemy knows a good deal,” Yi Junnian weighed it over and over. “You Tianxiao looks cunning, but he's really a stupid, conceited man who fancies he's grasped some clue. My guess is that when the enemy let us go in the end, the likeliest reason is that they believe Comrade ‘Old Kai’ escaped from the scene of the arrests, while the agent planted inside the Party was taken in.”

Yi Junnian sank into thought again. Anyone could be the one, he thought. He shook his head and said to Ling Wen: “Thinking on like this will get us nowhere. These comrades Old Fang called together, we know almost nothing about most of them. A man's secret lies buried deep in his history; the Party has been broken up again and again, and of the comrades still carrying on the fight, hardly any have worked together from the very beginning.

“In White-area work, and above all in secret underground work, the organization keeps no personal history files, for safety's sake. If it were possible, I think we should propose to the higher-ups that the past history of every comrade at that meeting be gone over thoroughly.”

Ling Wen watched him reach out and pick up the photograph from the tea table, and all at once felt a jarring unease. Never before had Old Yi touched this photograph of the two of them; every time, he had pretended not to see it. She sometimes felt this was just where the trouble lay between her and Old Yi, that there would always be a Long Dong standing between them.

“You've said before that Comrade Long Dong withdrew from Shanghai because the Party had been badly broken up, with many comrades arrested and not a few killed. Why didn't the organization have you withdraw along with him?”
“Our end here hadn't been broken up; the enemy never knew of this place. My work was internal liaison; I had contact with few people, and after I married Long Dong I mostly did back-office duty.”
“Was it because someone had turned traitor?”
“The whole organizational system was destroyed; it's hard to get to the bottom of it.”
Late in the night, Ling Wen gazed at Long Dong's photograph on the tea table, thinking how cruel the struggle was, cruel enough even to turn many people into something beyond recognition.
